How to actually use these skills

Installing is one command, and the rest of this site already covers it. The part nobody mentions is what happens after: most skills fire without you asking for them, the ones that don’t you call by name, and a job bigger than one edit wants a different opening move than a small one. This is the first session, in the order you’ll actually hit it.

Install it, if you haven’t

The install box on the landing page carries a prompt rather than a command — you paste it into whichever coding agent you use, and it works out which harness it’s in and takes that harness’s route. On Claude Code that route is a clone-or-pull into ~/.claude/skills/TBaguette, and nothing else on your machine is touched. Install verification is the page that proves that claim, with the actual test source rather than the claim restated in different words.

Reload — and know that the conversation you installed from won’t

A running agent holds the skill list it started with. Restart it — in Claude Code, /reload-plugins does it without a restart — and every new conversation picks the library up.

The conversation you ran the install from is the exception worth naming, because it’s the one you’re most likely to test in. It started before the install, so it still has the old list, and nothing you just did changes that. Open a new conversation, or invoke TBaguette:using-tbaguette in the old one to load the entry point by hand.

One more place this bites, on Claude specifically: this is Claude Code. The Claude Desktop app and claude.ai chat don’t read ~/.claude/skills/ at all — they load whatever is enabled on your account, synced separately — so cloning here will never make these show up there. Enable them from Customize in the Desktop sidebar or the skills settings on claude.ai instead.

Confirm it landed

Ask your agent to invoke TBaguette:using-tbaguette. If the install worked, it comes back with a short notice about checking skills before every response — that notice is the library’s entry point, and seeing it is proof the whole thing is loaded and callable, not just present on disk. If you get “no such skill” instead, the clone isn’t where your agent reads from, and the install prompt’s own verification steps will say which case you’re in.

Most of the time you won’t invoke anything

Every skill carries a trigger description — the situations it is for, written out at length rather than summarized into a category. Your agent matches what you are doing against those, and TBaguette:using-tbaguette is the piece that makes that check habitual rather than occasional.

So the ordinary experience is that you never type a skill name. You say fix this bug, and diagnosing-before-fixing arrives before a patch does — a reproduction first, then the cause, then the fix. You ask for an interface, and formidable turns up with the questions a designer would have asked. You do not have to memorize 92 names, and you should not try.

When you do want one by name

Invoke it directly — TBaguette:formidable, TBaguette:knowing-when-to-stop, whichever one you mean. There are two honest reasons to override the automatic path. The first is that you know your own situation better than a trigger description can: the work does not look like the skill’s trigger, but the discipline still applies. The second is timing — you want it before your agent has decided this task is simple enough to skip it, which is reliably the moment it is not.

Six worth trying on purpose

Not a ranking, and not the six that matter most — the six whose effect you can watch inside a single session, which makes them the fastest way to find out whether any of this is for you.

  • formidable — The flagship, and the one with the most visible before-and-after. Design craft for every stack there is — web, terminal, native, game HUD, print, voice — so it applies to the interface you actually have rather than the one a web tutorial assumed you had.
  • diagnosing-before-fixing — Turns fix this into a reproduction before a patch. The fastest way to see the difference: hand it a bug whose obvious fix you already have in mind, and watch where it goes first.
  • writing-the-failing-test-first — The most concrete behavior change on this list. One test that fails for the right reason before any production code exists — a different thing from a test written afterwards that has never once been red.
  • confirming-before-claiming-done — For anyone who has been told something was finished and found out otherwise. It replaces this should work with a command that was actually run, and treats a tool’s own success report as a claim rather than as evidence.
  • orchestrating-work-end-to-end — The entry point for anything bigger than a single edit — which is the next section, because it is the one piece of this that changes how a whole run is shaped rather than how one response is.
  • knowing-when-to-stop — The counterweight to everything above. Bounded passes, diminishing returns, and naming what is being left undone instead of quietly polishing until the context runs out.

Anything bigger than one edit starts somewhere else

One skill covers one stretch of work. A feature, a bug with no known cause, a migration, an audit — those take several of them, in an order, and that order is its own skill: orchestrating-work-end-to-end. It routes the request to the lightest track that fits, says which phase the work is in, and names the evidence that has to exist before the next phase is allowed to open.

The practical version, for you: describe what you want, and let it open with scoping rather than with an editor. What comes back first is a design to say yes or no to — which is a great deal cheaper to argue with than a finished implementation of the wrong thing.

Keeping it current

Run the same install prompt again — it takes whichever route it took the first time. On the Claude Code route that route is a clone-or-pull, so a second run updates in place rather than erroring, duplicating anything, or touching whatever else lives beside it. On a harness with its own plugin command, the prompt hands back to that command, and updating is whatever that harness already does.

Mostly you will not have to remember. keeping-tbaguette-current runs that check at the start of a conversation and reports what changed in readable terms rather than as a commit log. This site’s own header carries the published version and the moment it was last built, if you would rather compare by hand.

Not on Claude Code?

TBaguette ships an integration for Codex, Cursor, Copilot CLI, Devin, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Kimi Code, OpenCode, and Pi as well. Those installs differ in kind rather than just in path — a plugin command here, an extension there, a line in a config file somewhere else — which is exactly why the install box carries one prompt instead of ten recipes. It identifies its own harness and takes the matching route, and when it cannot identify one it stops and asks rather than inventing a path. PORTING.md has the harness-by-harness breakdown of what each one loads.

If nothing seems to be happening

Roughly in the order worth checking, cheapest first:

  • The conversation predates the install — including the one you installed from. Open a new one, or invoke TBaguette:using-tbaguette to load the entry point by hand.
  • You are in Claude Desktop or claude.ai chat, not Claude Code. Those load skills from your account rather than from ~/.claude/skills/, so nothing you cloned is visible to them.
  • Your agent has them and simply is not reaching for them. Invoke one by name. If that works, the install is fine and what you are watching is trigger matching — say what you are doing in plainer terms, or name the skill yourself.
  • The clone is not where your agent reads from. Check that ~/.claude/skills/TBaguette/CATALOG.md exists. If that directory is there but has no .git inside it, what you have is a previous install that lost its own history rather than a fresh one — the install prompt recognizes that case and asks before moving anything aside.

Where to go from here

Every skill on this site is readable in full and searchable by name, summary, or category, grouped into categories on the landing page. CATALOG.md is that same catalog as a single file, which is the better one to hand your agent when you want it to read rather than search.

TBaguette’s Atelier — the judgment calls that sit between the ticket and the commit, organized like a proper bench.
